333|## Union Passthrough
334|
335|_Found at {py:func}`cattrs.strategies.configure_union_passthrough`._
336|
337|The _union passthrough_ strategy enables a {py:class}`Converter <cattrs.BaseConverter>` to structure unions and subunions of given types.
338|
339|A very common use case for _cattrs_ is processing data created by other serialization libraries, such as _JSON_ or _msgpack_.
340|These libraries are able to directly produce values of unions inherent to the format.
341|For example, every JSON library can differentiate between numbers, booleans, strings and null values since these values are represented differently in the wire format.
342|This strategy enables _cattrs_ to offload the creation of these values to an underlying library and just validate the final value.
343|So, _cattrs_ preconfigured JSON converters can handle the following type:
344|
345|- `bool | int | float | str | None`
346|
347|Continuing the JSON example, this strategy also enables structuring subsets of unions of these values.
348|Accordingly, here are some examples of subset unions that are also supported:
349|
350|- `bool | int`
351|- `int | str`
352|- `int | float | str`
353|
354|The strategy also supports types including one or more [Literals](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/literal_types.html#literal-types) of supported types. For example:
355|
356|- `Literal["admin", "user"] | int`
357|- `Literal[True] | str | int | float`
358|
359|The strategy also supports [NewTypes](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/more_types.html#newtypes) of these types. For example:
360|
361|```python
362|>>> from typing import NewType
363|
364|>>> UserId = NewType("UserId", int)
365|
366|>>> converter.loads("12", UserId)
367|12
368|```
369|
370|```{versionchanged} 26.2.0
371|PEP 695 type aliases of supported types are supported when used as union members.
372|```
373|
374|Unions containing unsupported types can be handled if at least one union type is supported by the strategy; the supported union types will be checked before the rest (referred to as the _spillover_) is handed over to the converter again.
375|
376|For example, if `A` and `B` are arbitrary _attrs_ classes, the union `Literal[10] | A | B` cannot be handled directly by a JSON converter.
377|However, the strategy will check if the value being structured matches `Literal[10]` (because this type _is_ supported) and, if not, will pass it back to the converter to be structured as `A | B` (where a different strategy can handle it).
378|
379|The strategy is designed to run in _O(1)_ at structure time; it doesn't depend on the size of the union and the ordering of union members.
380|
381|This strategy has been preapplied to the following preconfigured converters:
382|
383|- {py:class}`BsonConverter <cattrs.preconf.bson.BsonConverter>`
384|- {py:class}`Cbor2Converter <cattrs.preconf.cbor2.Cbor2Converter>`
385|- {py:class}`JsonConverter <cattrs.preconf.json.JsonConverter>`
386|- {py:class}`MsgpackConverter <cattrs.preconf.msgpack.MsgpackConverter>`
387|- {py:class}`MsgspecJsonConverter <cattrs.preconf.msgspec.MsgspecJsonConverter>`
388|- {py:class}`OrjsonConverter <cattrs.preconf.orjson.OrjsonConverter>`
389|- {py:class}`PyyamlConverter <cattrs.preconf.pyyaml.PyyamlConverter>`
390|- {py:class}`TomlkitConverter <cattrs.preconf.tomlkit.TomlkitConverter>`
391|- {py:class}`UjsonConverter <cattrs.preconf.ujson.UjsonConverter>`
392|
393|```{versionadded} 23.2.0

71|            if is_subclass(args[0], str) and is_subclass(args[0], Enum):
72|
73|                def key_handler(v):
74|                    return v.value
75|
76|            else:

78|                # (For example base85 encoding for bytes.)
79|                # In that case, we want to use the override.
80|
81|                kh = converter.get_unstructure_hook(args[0])
82|                if kh != identity:
83|                    key_handler = kh
84|
85|        return converter.gen_unstructure_mapping(

87|        )

1|# Preconfigured Converters
2|
3|The {mod}`cattrs.preconf` package contains factories for preconfigured converters, specifically adjusted for particular serialization libraries.
4|
5|For example, to get a converter configured for _orjson_:
6|
7|```{doctest}
8|
9|>>> from cattrs.preconf.orjson import make_converter
10|
11|>>> converter = make_converter() # Takes the same parameters as the `cattrs.Converter`
12|```
13|
14|Converters obtained this way can be customized further, just like any other converter.
15|
16|For compatibility and performance reasons, these converters are usually configured to unstructure differently than ordinary `Converters`.
17|A couple of examples:
18|* the {class}`_orjson_ converter <cattrs.preconf.orjson.OrjsonConverter>` is configured to pass `datetime` instances unstructured since _orjson_ can handle them faster.
19|* the {class}`_msgspec_ JSON converter <cattrs.preconf.msgspec.MsgspecJsonConverter>` is configured to pass through some dataclasses and _attrs_classes,
20|if the output is identical to what normal unstructuring would have produced, since _msgspec_ can handle them faster.
21|
22|The intended usage is to pass the unstructured output directly to the underlying library,
23|or use `converter.dumps` which will do it for you.
24|
25|These converters support all [default hooks](defaulthooks.md)
26|and the following additional classes and type annotations,
27|both for structuring and unstructuring:
28|
29|- `datetime.datetime`, `datetime.date`
30|
31|```{versionadded} 22.1.0
32|All preconf converters now have `loads` and `dumps` methods, which combine un/structuring and the de/serialization logic from their underlying libraries.
33|```
34|
35|```{doctest}
36|
37|>>> from cattrs.preconf.json import make_converter
38|
39|>>> converter = make_converter()
40|
41|>>> @define
42|... class Test:
43|...     a: int
44|
45|>>> converter.dumps(Test(1))
46|'{"a": 1}'
47|```
48|
49|Particular libraries may have additional constraints documented below.
50|
51|Third-party libraries can be specified as optional (extra) dependencies on _cattrs_ during installation.
52|Optional install targets should match the name of the {mod}`cattrs.preconf` modules.
53|
54|```console
55|# Using pip
56|$ pip install cattrs[ujson]
57|
58|# Usinv uv
59|$ uv add cattrs[msgspec]
60|
61|# Using pdm
62|$ pdm add cattrs[orjson]
63|
64|# Using poetry
65|$ poetry add --extras tomlkit cattrs
66|```
67|
68|
69|## Standard Library _json_
70|
71|Found at {mod}`cattrs.preconf.json`.
72|
73|Bytes are serialized as base 85 strings. Counters are serialized as dictionaries. Sets are serialized as lists, and deserialized back into sets. `datetime` s and `date` s are serialized as ISO 8601 strings.
74|
75|
76|## _orjson_
77|
78|Found at {mod}`cattrs.preconf.orjson`.
79|
80|Bytes are un/structured as base 85 strings.
81|Sets are unstructured into lists, and structured back into sets.
82|`datetime` s and `date` s are passed through to be unstructured into RFC 3339 by _orjson_ itself.
83|Typed named tuples are unstructured into ordinary tuples, and then into JSON arrays by _orjson_.
84|
85|_orjson_ doesn't support integers less than -9223372036854775808, and greater than 9223372036854775807.
86|_orjson_ only supports mappings with string keys so mappings will have their keys stringified before serialization, and destringified during deserialization.
87|
88|
89|## _msgspec_
90|
91|Found at {mod}`cattrs.preconf.msgspec`.
92|Only JSON functionality is currently available, other formats supported by msgspec to follow in the future.
93|
94|[_msgspec_ structs](https://jcristharif.com/msgspec/structs.html) are supported, but not composable - a struct will be handed over to _msgspec_ directly, and _msgspec_ will handle and all of its fields, recursively.
95|_cattrs_ may get more sophisticated handling of structs in the future.
96|
97|[_msgspec_ strict mode](https://jcristharif.com/msgspec/usage.html#strict-vs-lax-mode) is used by default.
98|This can be customized by changing the {meth}`encoder <cattrs.preconf.msgspec.MsgspecJsonConverter.encoder>` attribute on the converter.
99|
100|What _cattrs_ calls _unstructuring_ and _structuring_, _msgspec_ calls [`to_builtins` and `convert`](https://jcristharif.com/msgspec/converters.html).
101|What _cattrs_ refers to as _dumping_ and _loading_, _msgspec_ refers to as [`encoding` and `decoding`](https://jcristharif.com/msgspec/usage.html).
102|
103|Compatibility notes:
104|- Bytes are un/structured as base 64 strings directly by _msgspec_ itself.
105|- _msgspec_ [encodes special float values](https://jcristharif.com/msgspec/supported-types.html#float) (`NaN, Inf, -Inf`) as `null`.
106|- `datetime` s and `date` s are passed through to be unstructured into RFC 3339 by _msgspec_ itself.
107|- _attrs_ classes, dataclasses and sequences are handled directly by _msgspec_ if possible, otherwise by the normal _cattrs_ machinery.
108|This means it's possible the validation errors produced may be _msgspec_ validation errors instead of _cattrs_ validation errors.
109|
110|This converter supports {meth}`get_loads_hook() <cattrs.preconf.msgspec.MsgspecJsonConverter.get_loads_hook>` and {meth}`get_dumps_hook() <cattrs.preconf.msgspec.MsgspecJsonConverter.get_dumps_hook>`.
111|These are factories for dumping and loading functions (as opposed to unstructuring and structuring); the hooks returned by this may be further optimized to offload as much work as possible to _msgspec_.
112|
113|```python
114|>>> from cattrs.preconf.msgspec import make_converter
115|
116|>>> @define
117|... class Test:
118|...     a: int
119|
120|>>> converter = make_converter()
121|>>> dumps = converter.get_dumps_hook(A)
122|
123|>>> dumps(Test(1))  # Will use msgspec directly.
124|b'{"a":1}'
125|```
126|
127|Due to its complexity, this converter is currently _provisional_ and may slightly change as the best integration patterns are discovered.
128|
129|_msgspec_ doesn't support PyPy.
130|
131|```{versionadded} 24.1.0
132|
133|```
134|
135|
136|## _tomllib_
137|
138|Found at {mod}`cattrs.preconf.tomllib`.
139|
140|Bytes are serialized as base 85 strings. Sets are serialized as lists, and deserialized back into sets.
141|Tuples are serialized as lists, and deserialized back into tuples.
142|_tomllib_ only supports mappings with string keys so mappings will have their keys stringified before serialization, and destringified during deserialization.
143|
144|Writing is supported via the [_tomli-w_](https://pypi.org/project/tomli-w/) library; this needs to be installed separately (or depend on the `cattrs[tomllib]` extra).
145|
146|On Python 3.10, the [_tomli_](https://pypi.org/project/tomli/) library is required.
147|
148|```{versionadded} 26.1.0
149|
150|```
151|
152|
153|## _ujson_
154|
155|Found at {mod}`cattrs.preconf.ujson`.
156|
157|Bytes are serialized as base 85 strings. Sets are serialized as lists, and deserialized back into sets. `datetime` s and `date` s are serialized as ISO 8601 strings.
158|
159|_ujson_ doesn't support integers less than -9223372036854775808, and greater than 9223372036854775807, nor does it support `float('inf')`.
160|
161|
162|## _msgpack_
163|
164|Found at {mod}`cattrs.preconf.msgpack`.
165|
166|Sets are serialized as lists, and deserialized back into sets. `datetime` s are serialized as UNIX timestamp float values. `date` s are serialized as midnight-aligned UNIX timestamp float values.
167|Naive `datetime` s are assumed to be UTC, which is also how timestamps are interpreted when structuring.
168|
169|```{versionchanged} 26.2.0
170|Naive `datetime` s are assumed to be UTC when unstructuring.
171|They were previously interpreted as local time, making the serialized value depend on the timezone of the machine doing the unstructuring.
172|```
173|
174|_msgpack_ doesn't support integers less than -9223372036854775808, and greater than 18446744073709551615.
175|
176|When parsing msgpack data from bytes, the library needs to be passed `strict_map_key=False` to get the full range of compatibility.
177|
178|
179|## _cbor2_
180|
181|Found at {mod}`cattrs.preconf.cbor2`.
182|
183|_cbor2_ implements a fully featured CBOR encoder with several extensions for handling shared references, big integers, rational numbers and so on.
184|
185|Sets are serialized and deserialized to sets.
186|Tuples are serialized as lists.
187|
188|`datetime` s are serialized as a text string by default (CBOR Tag 0).
189|Use keyword argument `datetime_as_timestamp=True` to encode as UNIX timestamp integer/float (CBOR Tag 1)
190|**note:** this replaces timezone information as UTC.
191|Naive `datetime` s are assumed to be UTC, which is also how timestamps are interpreted when structuring.
192|
193|```{versionchanged} 26.2.0
194|Naive `datetime` s are assumed to be UTC when unstructuring.
195|They were previously interpreted as local time, making the serialized value depend on the timezone of the machine doing the unstructuring.
196|```
197|
198|`date` s are serialized as ISO 8601 strings.
199|
200|Use keyword argument `canonical=True` for efficient encoding to the smallest binary output.
201|
202|Floats can be forced to smaller output by casting to lower-precision formats by casting to `numpy` floats (and back to Python floats).
203|Example: `float(np.float32(value))` or `float(np.float16(value))`
204|
205|```{versionadded} 23.1.0
206|
207|```
208|
209|## _bson_
210|
211|Found at {mod}`cattrs.preconf.bson`. Tested against the _bson_ module bundled with the _pymongo_ library, not the standalone PyPI _bson_ package.
212|
213|Sets are serialized as lists, and deserialized back into sets.
214|
215|_bson_ doesn't support integers less than -9223372036854775808 or greater than 9223372036854775807 (64-bit signed).
216|_bson_ does not support null bytes in mapping keys.
217|_bson_ only supports mappings with string keys so mappings will have their keys stringified before serialization, and destringified during deserialization.
218|The _bson_ datetime representation doesn't support microsecond accuracy.
219|`date` s are serialized as ISO 8601 strings.
220|
221|When encoding and decoding, the library needs to be passed `codec_options=bson.CodecOptions(tz_aware=True)` to get the full range of compatibility.
222|
223|
224|## _pyyaml_
225|
226|Found at {mod}`cattrs.preconf.pyyaml`.
227|
228|Frozensets are serialized as lists, and deserialized back into frozensets.
229|`date` s are serialized as ISO 8601 strings.
230|Typed named tuples are unstructured into ordinary tuples, and then into YAML arrays by _pyyaml_.
231|
232|## _tomlkit_
233|
234|Found at {mod}`cattrs.preconf.tomlkit`.
235|
236|Bytes are serialized as base 85 strings. Sets are serialized as lists, and deserialized back into sets.
237|Tuples are serialized as lists, and deserialized back into tuples.
238|_tomlkit_ only supports mappings with string keys so mappings will have their keys stringified before serialization, and destringified during deserialization.
239|[`date`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.date) and [`datetime`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime) objects are passed through to be unstructured by _tomlkit_ itself.

1|"""Cattrs validation."""
2|
3|from typing import Callable, Union
4|
5|from .errors import (
6|    ClassValidationError,
7|    ForbiddenExtraKeysError,
8|    IterableValidationError,
9|)
10|
11|__all__ = ["format_exception", "transform_error"]
12|
13|
14|def format_exception(exc: BaseException, type: Union[type, None]) -> str:
15|    """The default exception formatter, handling the most common exceptions.
16|
17|    The following exceptions are handled specially:
18|
19|    * `KeyErrors` (`required field missing`)
20|    * `ValueErrors` (`invalid value for type, expected <type>` or just `invalid value`)
21|    * `TypeErrors` (`invalid value for type, expected <type>` and a couple special
22|      cases for iterables)
23|    * `cattrs.ForbiddenExtraKeysError`
24|    * some `AttributeErrors` (special cased for structing mappings)
25|    """
26|    if isinstance(exc, KeyError):
27|        res = "required field missing"
28|    elif isinstance(exc, ValueError):
29|        if type is not None:
30|            tn = type.__name__ if hasattr(type, "__name__") else repr(type)
31|            res = f"invalid value for type, expected {tn}"
32|        else:
33|            res = "invalid value"
34|    elif isinstance(exc, TypeError):
35|        if type is None:
36|            if exc.args[0].endswith("object is not iterable"):
37|                res = "invalid value for type, expected an iterable"
38|            else:
39|                res = f"invalid type ({exc})"
40|        else:
41|            tn = type.__name__ if hasattr(type, "__name__") else repr(type)
42|            res = f"invalid value for type, expected {tn}"
43|    elif isinstance(exc, ForbiddenExtraKeysError):
44|        res = f"extra fields found ({', '.join(sorted(exc.extra_fields))})"
45|    elif isinstance(exc, AttributeError) and exc.args[0].endswith(
46|        "object has no attribute 'items'"
47|    ):
48|        # This was supposed to be a mapping (and have .items()) but it something else.
49|        res = "expected a mapping"
50|    else:
51|        res = f"unknown error ({exc})"
52|
53|    return res
54|
55|
56|def transform_error(
57|    exc: Union[ClassValidationError, IterableValidationError, BaseException],
58|    path: str = "$",
59|    format_exception: Callable[
60|        [BaseException, Union[type, None]], str
61|    ] = format_exception,
62|) -> list[str]:
63|    """Transform an exception into a list of error messages.
64|
65|    To get detailed error messages, the exception should be produced by a converter
66|    with `detailed_validation` set.
67|
68|    By default, the error messages are in the form of `{description} @ {path}`.
69|
70|    While traversing the exception and subexceptions, the path is formed:
71|
72|    * by appending `.{field_name}` for fields in classes
73|    * by appending `[{int}]` for indices in iterables, like lists
74|    * by appending `[{str}]` for keys in mappings, like dictionaries
75|
76|    :param exc: The exception to transform into error messages.
77|    :param path: The root path to use.
78|    :param format_exception: A callable to use to transform `Exceptions` into
79|        string descriptions of errors.
80|
81|    .. versionadded:: 23.1.0
82|    """
83|    errors = []
84|    if isinstance(exc, IterableValidationError):
85|        with_notes, without = exc.group_exceptions()
86|        for exc, note in with_notes:
87|            p = f"{path}[{note.index!r}]"
88|            if isinstance(exc, (ClassValidationError, IterableValidationError)):
89|                errors.extend(transform_error(exc, p, format_exception))
90|            else:
91|                errors.append(f"{format_exception(exc, note.type)} @ {p}")
92|        for exc in without:
93|            errors.append(f"{format_exception(exc, None)} @ {path}")
94|    elif isinstance(exc, ClassValidationError):
95|        with_notes, without = exc.group_exceptions()
96|        for exc, note in with_notes:
97|            p = f"{path}.{note.name}"
98|            if isinstance(exc, (ClassValidationError, IterableValidationError)):
99|                errors.extend(transform_error(exc, p, format_exception))
100|            else:
101|                errors.append(f"{format_exception(exc, note.type)} @ {p}")
102|        for exc in without:
103|            errors.append(f"{format_exception(exc, None)} @ {path}")
104|    else:
105|        errors.append(f"{format_exception(exc, None)} @ {path}")
106|    return errors

1|# Advanced Examples
2|
3|This section covers advanced use examples of _cattrs_ features.
4|
5|## Using Factory Hooks
6|
7|For this example, let's assume you have some attrs classes with snake case attributes, and you want to un/structure them as camel case.
8|
9|```{warning}
10|A simpler and better approach to this problem is to simply make your class attributes camel case.
11|However, this is a good example of the power of hook factories and _cattrs'_ composition-based design.
12|```
13|
14|Here's our simple data model:
15|
16|```python
17|@define
18|class Inner:
19|    a_snake_case_int: int
20|    a_snake_case_float: float
21|    a_snake_case_str: str
22|
23|@define
24|class Outer:
25|    a_snake_case_inner: Inner
26|```
27|
28|Let's examine our options one by one, starting with the simplest: writing manual un/structuring hooks.
29|
30|We just write the code by hand and register it:
31|
32|```python
33|def unstructure_inner(inner):
34|    return {
35|        "aSnakeCaseInt": inner.a_snake_case_int,
36|        "aSnakeCaseFloat": inner.a_snake_case_float,
37|        "aSnakeCaseStr": inner.a_snake_case_str
38|    }
39|
40|>>> converter.register_unstructure_hook(Inner, unstructure_inner)
41|```
42|
43|(Let's skip the other unstructure hook and 2 structure hooks due to verbosity.)
44|
45|This will get us where we want to go, but the drawbacks are immediately obvious:
46|we'd need to write a ton of code ourselves, wasting effort, increasing our
47|maintenance burden and risking bugs. Obviously this won't do.
48|
49|Why write code when we can write code to write code for us? In this case this
50|code has already been written for you. _cattrs_ contains a module,
51|{mod}`cattrs.gen`, with functions to automatically generate hooks exactly like this.
52|These functions also take parameters to customize the generated hooks.
53|
54|We can generate and register the renaming hooks we need:
55|
56|```python
57|>>> from cattrs.gen import make_dict_unstructure_fn, override
58|
59|>>> converter.register_unstructure_hook(
60|...     Inner,
61|...      make_dict_unstructure_fn(
62|...          Inner,
63|...          converter,
64|...          a_snake_case_int=override(rename="aSnakeCaseInt"),
65|...          a_snake_case_float=override(rename="aSnakeCaseFloat"),
66|...          a_snake_case_str=override(rename="aSnakeCaseStr"),
67|...      )
68|...  )
69|```
70|
71|(Again skipping the other hooks due to verbosity.)
72|
73|This is still too verbose and manual for our tastes, so let's automate it
74|further. We need a way to convert snake case identifiers to camel case, so
75|let's grab one from Stack Overflow:
76|
77|```python
78|def to_camel_case(snake_str: str) -> str:
79|    components = snake_str.split("_")
80|    return components[0] + "".join(x.title() for x in components[1:])
81|```
82|
83|We can combine this with [`attrs.fields`](https://www.attrs.org/en/stable/api.html#attrs.fields) to save us some typing:
84|
85|```python
86|from attrs import fields
87|from cattrs.gen import make_dict_unstructure_fn, override
88|
89|converter.register_unstructure_hook(
90|    Inner,
91|    make_dict_unstructure_fn(
92|        Inner,
93|        converter,
94|        **{a.name: override(rename=to_camel_case(a.name)) for a in fields(Inner)}
95|    )
96|)
97|
98|converter.register_unstructure_hook(
99|    Outer,
100|    make_dict_unstructure_fn(
101|        Outer,
102|        converter,
103|        **{a.name: override(rename=to_camel_case(a.name)) for a in fields(Outer)}
104|    )
105|)
106|```
107|
108|(Skipping the structuring hooks due to verbosity.)
109|
110|Now we're getting somewhere, but we still need to do this for each class
111|separately. The final step is using hook factories instead of hooks directly.
112|
113|Hook factories are functions that return hooks. They are also registered using
114|predicates instead of being attached to classes directly, like normal
115|un/structure hooks. Predicates are functions that given a type return a
116|boolean whether they handle it.
117|
118|We want our hook factories to trigger for all _attrs_ classes, so we need a
119|predicate to recognize whether a type is an _attrs_ class. Luckily, _attrs_ comes
120|with [`attrs.has`](https://www.attrs.org/en/stable/api.html#attrs.has), which is exactly this.
121|
122|As the final step, we can combine all of this into two hook factories:
123|
124|```python
125|from attrs import has, fields
126|from cattrs import Converter
127|from cattrs.gen import make_dict_unstructure_fn, make_dict_structure_fn, override
128|
129|converter = Converter()
130|
131|def to_camel_case(snake_str: str) -> str:
132|    components = snake_str.split("_")
133|    return components[0] + "".join(x.title() for x in components[1:])
134|
135|def to_camel_case_unstructure(cls):
136|    return make_dict_unstructure_fn(
137|        cls,
138|        converter,
139|        **{
140|            a.name: override(rename=to_camel_case(a.name))
141|            for a in fields(cls)
142|        }
143|    )
144|
145|def to_camel_case_structure(cls):
146|    return make_dict_structure_fn(
147|        cls,
148|        converter,
149|        **{
150|            a.name: override(rename=to_camel_case(a.name))
151|            for a in fields(cls)
152|        }
153|    )
154|
155|converter.register_unstructure_hook_factory(
156|    has, to_camel_case_unstructure
157|)
158|converter.register_structure_hook_factory(
159|    has, to_camel_case_structure
160|)
161|```
162|
163|The `converter` instance will now un/structure every attrs class to camel case.
164|Nothing has been omitted from this final example; it's complete.
165|
166|
167|## Using Fallback Key Names
168|
169|Sometimes when structuring data, the input data may be in multiple formats that need to be converted into a common attribute.
170|
171|Consider an example where a data store creates a new schema version and renames a key (ie, `{'old_field':  'value1'}` in v1 becomes `{'new_field': 'value1'}` in v2), while also leaving existing records in the system with the V1 schema. Both keys should convert to the same field.
172|
173|Here, builtin customizations such as [rename](./customizing.md#rename) are insufficient - _cattrs_ cannot structure both `old_field` and `new_field` into a single field using `rename`, at least not on the same converter.
174|
175|In order to support both fields, you can apply a little preprocessing to the default _cattrs_ structuring hooks.
176|One approach is to write the following decorator and apply it to your class.
177|
178|```python
179|from attrs import define
180|from cattrs import Converter
181|from cattrs.gen import make_dict_structure_fn
182|
183|converter = Converter()
184|
185|
186|def fallback_field(
187|    converter_arg: Converter,
188|    old_to_new_field: dict[str, str]
189|):
190|    def decorator(cls):
191|        struct = make_dict_structure_fn(cls, converter_arg)
192|
193|        def structure(d, cl):
194|            for k, v in old_to_new_field.items():
195|                if k in d:
196|                    d[v] = d[k]
197|
198|            return struct(d, cl)
199|
200|        converter_arg.register_structure_hook(cls, structure)
201|
202|        return cls
203|
204|    return decorator
205|
206|
207|@fallback_field(converter, {"old_field": "new_field"})
208|@define
209|class MyInternalAttr:
210|    new_field: str
211|```
212|
213|_cattrs_ will now structure both key names into `new_field` on your class.
214|
215|```python
216|converter.structure({"new_field": "foo"}, MyInternalAttr)
217|converter.structure({"old_field": "foo"}, MyInternalAttr)
218|```

43|    * counters are serialized as dicts
44|    * sets are serialized as lists
45|    * string and int enums are passed through when unstructuring

51|    """

54|    )
55|    converter.register_structure_hook(bytes, lambda v, _: b85decode(v))
56|    converter.register_unstructure_hook(datetime, lambda v: v.isoformat())
57|    converter.register_structure_hook(datetime, lambda v, _: datetime.fromisoformat(v))
58|    converter.register_unstructure_hook(date, lambda v: v.isoformat())
59|    converter.register_structure_hook(date, lambda v, _: date.fromisoformat(v))

62|    )

1|# *cattrs*: Flexible Object Serialization and Validation
2|
3|*Because validation belongs to the edges.*
4|
5|[![Documentation](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docs-Read%20The%20Docs-black)](https://catt.rs/)
6|[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-C06524)](https://github.com/hynek/stamina/blob/main/LICENSE)
7|[![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/cattrs.svg)](https://pypi.python.org/pypi/cattrs)
8|[![Supported Python Versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/cattrs.svg)](https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs)
9|[![Downloads](https://static.pepy.tech/badge/cattrs/month)](https://pepy.tech/project/cattrs)
10|[![Coverage](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/Tinche/22405310d6a663164d894a2beab4d44d/raw/covbadge.json)](https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs/actions/workflows/main.yml)
11|
12|---
13|
14|<!-- begin-teaser -->
15|
16|**cattrs** is a Swiss Army knife for (un)structuring and validating data in Python.
17|In practice, that means it converts **unstructured dictionaries** into **proper classes** and back, while **validating** their contents.
18|
19|<!-- end-teaser -->
20|
21|
22|## Example
23|
24|<!-- begin-example -->
25|
26|_cattrs_ works best with [_attrs_](https://www.attrs.org/) classes, and [dataclasses](https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html) where simple (un-)structuring works out of the box, even for nested data, without polluting your data model with serialization details:
27|
28|```python
29|>>> from attrs import define
30|>>> from cattrs import structure, unstructure
31|>>> @define
32|... class C:
33|...     a: int
34|...     b: list[str]
35|>>> instance = structure({'a': 1, 'b': ['x', 'y']}, C)
36|>>> instance
37|C(a=1, b=['x', 'y'])
38|>>> unstructure(instance)
39|{'a': 1, 'b': ['x', 'y']}
40|```
41|
42|<!-- end-teaser -->
43|<!-- end-example -->
44|
45|Have a look at [*Why *cattrs*?*](https://catt.rs/en/latest/why.html) for more examples!
46|
47|<!-- begin-why -->
48|
49|## Features
50|
51|### Recursive Unstructuring
52|
53|- _attrs_ classes and dataclasses are converted into dictionaries in a way similar to `attrs.asdict()`, or into tuples in a way similar to `attrs.astuple()`.
54|- Enumeration instances are converted to their values.
55|- Other types are let through without conversion. This includes types such as integers, dictionaries, lists and instances of non-_attrs_ classes.
56|- Custom converters for any type can be registered using `register_unstructure_hook`.
57|
58|
59|### Recursive Structuring
60|
61|Converts unstructured data into structured data, recursively, according to your specification given as a type.
62|The following types are supported:
63|
64|- `typing.Optional[T]` and its 3.10+ form, `T | None`.
65|- `list[T]`, `typing.List[T]`, `typing.MutableSequence[T]`, `typing.Sequence[T]` convert to lists.
66|- `tuple` and `typing.Tuple` (both variants, `tuple[T, ...]` and `tuple[X, Y, Z]`).
67|- `set[T]`, `typing.MutableSet[T]`, and `typing.Set[T]` convert to sets.
68|- `frozenset[T]`, and `typing.FrozenSet[T]` convert to frozensets.
69|- `dict[K, V]`, `typing.Dict[K, V]`, `typing.MutableMapping[K, V]`, and `typing.Mapping[K, V]` convert to dictionaries.
70|- [`typing.TypedDict`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.TypedDict), both ordinary and generic.
71|- [`typing.NewType`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#newtype)
72|- [PEP 695 type aliases](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#type-aliases) on 3.12+
73|- _attrs_ classes with simple attributes and the usual `__init__`[^simple].
74|- All _attrs_ classes and dataclasses with the usual `__init__`, if their complex attributes have type metadata.
75|- Unions of supported _attrs_ classes, given that all of the classes have a unique field.
76|- Unions of anything, if you provide a disambiguation function for it.
77|- Custom converters for any type can be registered using `register_structure_hook`.
78|
79|[^simple]: Simple attributes are attributes that can be assigned unstructured data, like numbers, strings, and collections of unstructured data.
80|
81|
82|### Batteries Included
83|
84|_cattrs_ comes with pre-configured converters for a number of serialization libraries, including JSON (standard library, [_orjson_](https://pypi.org/project/orjson/), [UltraJSON](https://pypi.org/project/ujson/)), [_msgpack_](https://pypi.org/project/msgpack/), [_cbor2_](https://pypi.org/project/cbor2/), [_bson_](https://pypi.org/project/bson/), [PyYAML](https://pypi.org/project/PyYAML/), [_tomlkit_](https://pypi.org/project/tomlkit/) and [_msgspec_](https://pypi.org/project/msgspec/) (supports only JSON at this time).
85|
86|For details, see the [cattrs.preconf package](https://catt.rs/en/stable/preconf.html).
87|
88|
89|## Design Decisions
90|
91|_cattrs_ is based on a few fundamental design decisions:
92|
93|- Un/structuring rules are separate from the models.
94|  This allows models to have a one-to-many relationship with un/structuring rules, and to create un/structuring rules for models which you do not own and you cannot change.
95|  (_cattrs_ can be configured to use un/structuring rules from models using the [`use_class_methods` strategy](https://catt.rs/en/latest/strategies.html#using-class-specific-structure-and-unstructure-methods).)
96|- Invent as little as possible; reuse existing ordinary Python instead.
97|  For example, _cattrs_ did not have a custom exception type to group exceptions until the sanctioned Python [`exceptiongroups`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#ExceptionGroup).
98|  A side-effect of this design decision is that, in a lot of cases, when you're solving _cattrs_ problems you're actually learning Python instead of learning _cattrs_.
99|- Resist the temptation to guess.
100|  If there are two ways of solving a problem, _cattrs_ should refuse to guess and let the user configure it themselves.
101|
102|A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds, so these decisions can and are sometimes broken, but they have proven to be a good foundation.
103|
104|

1|# Converters In-Depth
2|```{currentmodule} cattrs
3|```
4|
5|Converters are registries of rules _cattrs_ uses to perform function composition and generate its un/structuring functions.
6|
7|Currently, a converter contains the following state:
8|
9|- a registry of unstructure hooks, backed by a [singledispatch](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.singledispatch) and a {class}`FunctionDispatch <cattrs.dispatch.FunctionDispatch>`, wrapped in a [cache](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.cache).
10|- a registry of structure hooks, backed by a different singledispatch and `FunctionDispatch`, and a different cache.
11|- a `detailed_validation` flag (defaulting to true), determining whether the converter uses [detailed validation](validation.md#detailed-validation).
12|- a reference to {class}`an unstructuring strategy <cattrs.UnstructureStrategy>` (either AS_DICT or AS_TUPLE).
13|- a `prefer_attrib_converters` flag (defaulting to false), determining whether to favor _attrs_ converters over normal _cattrs_ machinery when structuring _attrs_ classes
14|- a `dict_factory` callable, a legacy parameter used for creating `dicts` when dumping _attrs_ classes using `AS_DICT`.
15|
16|Converters may be cloned using the {meth}`Converter.copy() <cattrs.BaseConverter.copy>` method.
17|The new copy may be changed through the `copy` arguments, but will retain all manually registered hooks from the original.
18|
19|
20|## Customizing Collection Unstructuring
21|
22|```{tip}
23|See [](customizing.md#customizing-collections) for a more modern and more powerful way of customizing collection handling.
24|```
25|
26|Overriding collection unstructuring in a generic way can be a very useful feature.
27|A common example is using a JSON library that doesn't support sets, but expects lists and tuples instead.
28|
29|Using ordinary unstructuring hooks for this is unwieldy due to the semantics of
30|[singledispatch](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.singledispatch);
31|in other words, you'd need to register hooks for all specific types of set you're using (`set[int]`, `set[float]`,
32|`set[str]`...), which is not useful.
33|
34|Function-based hooks can be used instead, but come with their own set of challenges - they're complicated to write efficiently.
35|
36|The {class}`Converter` supports easy customizations of collection unstructuring using its `unstruct_collection_overrides` parameter.
37|For example, to unstructure all sets into lists, use the following:
38|
39|```{doctest}
40|
41|>>> from collections.abc import Set
42|>>> converter = cattrs.Converter(unstruct_collection_overrides={Set: list})
43|
44|>>> converter.unstructure({1, 2, 3})
45|[1, 2, 3]
46|```
47|
48|Going even further, the `Converter` contains heuristics to support the following Python types, in order of decreasing generality:
49|
50|- `typing.Sequence`, `typing.MutableSequence`, `list`, `deque`, `tuple`
51|- `typing.Set`, `frozenset`, `typing.MutableSet`, `set`
52|- `typing.Mapping`, `typing.MutableMapping`, `dict`, `defaultdict`, `collections.OrderedDict`, `collections.Counter`
53|
54|For example, if you override the unstructure type for `Sequence`, but not for `MutableSequence`, `list` or `tuple`, the override will also affect those types.
55|An easy way to remember the rule:
56|
57|- all `MutableSequence` s are `Sequence` s, so the override will apply
58|- all `list` s are `MutableSequence` s, so the override will apply
59|- all `tuple` s are `Sequence` s, so the override will apply
60|
61|If, however, you override only `MutableSequence`, fields annotated as `Sequence` will not be affected (since not all sequences are mutable sequences), and fields annotated as tuples will not be affected (since tuples
62|are not mutable sequences in the first place).
63|
64|Similar logic applies to the set and mapping hierarchies.
65|
66|Make sure you're using the types from `collections.abc` on Python 3.9+, and from `typing` on older Python versions.
67|
68|
69|## Fallback Hook Factories
70|
71|By default, when a {class}`converter <cattrs.BaseConverter>` cannot handle a type it will:
72|
73|* when unstructuring, pass the value through unchanged
74|* when structuring, raise a {class}`cattrs.errors.StructureHandlerNotFoundError` asking the user to add configuration
75|
76|These behaviors can be customized by providing custom [hook factories](usage.md#using-factory-hooks) when creating the converter.
77|
78|```python
79|>>> from pickle import dumps
80|
81|>>> class Unsupported:
82|...     """An artisinal (non-attrs) class, unsupported by default."""
83|
84|>>> converter = Converter(unstructure_fallback_factory=lambda _: dumps)
85|>>> instance = Unsupported()
86|>>> converter.unstructure(instance)
87|b'\x80\x04\x95\x18\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x8c\x08__main__\x94\x8c\x04Test\x94\x93\x94)\x81\x94.'
88|```
89|
90|This also enables converters to be chained.
91|
92|```python
93|>>> parent = Converter()
94|
95|>>> child = Converter(
96|...     unstructure_fallback_factory=parent.get_unstructure_hook,
97|...     structure_fallback_factory=parent.get_structure_hook,
98|... )
99|```
100|
101|```{versionadded} 23.2.0
102|
103|```
104|
105|## `cattrs.Converter`
106|
107|The {class}`Converter` is a converter variant that automatically generates, compiles and caches specialized structuring and unstructuring hooks for _attrs_ classes, dataclasses and TypedDicts.
108|
109|`Converter` differs from the {class}`cattrs.BaseConverter` in the following ways:
110|
111|- structuring and unstructuring of _attrs_ classes is slower the first time, but faster every subsequent time
112|- structuring and unstructuring can be customized
113|- support for _attrs_ classes with PEP563 (postponed) annotations
114|- support for generic _attrs_ classes
115|- support for easy overriding collection unstructuring
116|
117|The {class}`Converter` used to be called `GenConverter`, and that alias is still present for backwards compatibility.
118|
119|## `cattrs.BaseConverter`
120|
121|The {class}`BaseConverter` is a simpler and slower converter variant.
122|It does no code generation, so it may be faster on first-use which can be useful in specific cases, like CLI applications where startup time is more important than throughput.

1|# Validation
2|
3|_cattrs_ has a detailed validation mode since version 22.1.0, and this mode is enabled by default.
4|When running under detailed validation, the structuring hooks are slightly slower but produce richer and more precise error messages.
5|Unstructuring hooks are not affected.
6|
7|## Detailed Validation
8|
9|```{versionadded} 22.1.0
10|
11|```
12|In detailed validation mode, any structuring errors will be grouped and raised together as a {class}`cattrs.BaseValidationError`, which is a [PEP 654 ExceptionGroup](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0654/).
13|ExceptionGroups are special exceptions which contain lists of other exceptions, which may themselves be other ExceptionGroups.
14|In essence, ExceptionGroups are trees of exceptions.
15|
16|When structuring a class, _cattrs_ will gather any exceptions on a field-by-field basis and raise them as a {class}`cattrs.ClassValidationError`, which is a subclass of {class}`BaseValidationError <cattrs.BaseValidationError>`.
17|
18|When structuring sequences and mappings, _cattrs_ will gather any exceptions on a key- or index-basis and raise them as a {class}`cattrs.IterableValidationError`, which is a subclass of {class}`BaseValidationError <cattrs.BaseValidationError>`.
19|
20|The exceptions will also have their `__notes__` attributes set, as per [PEP 678](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0678/), showing the field, key or index for each inner exception.
21|
22|A simple example involving a class containing a list and a dictionary:
23|
24|```python
25|@define
26|class Class:
27|    a_list: list[int]
28|    a_dict: dict[str, int]
29|

32|  |   File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
33|  |   File "/Users/tintvrtkovic/pg/cattrs/src/cattr/converters.py", line 276, in structure

69|
70|### Transforming Exceptions into Error Messages
71|
72|```{versionadded} 23.1.0
73|
74|```
75|
76|ExceptionGroup stack traces are useful while developing, but sometimes a more compact representation of validation errors is required.
77|_cattrs_ provides a helper function, {func}`cattrs.transform_error`, which transforms validation errors into lists of error messages.
78|
79|The example from the previous paragraph produces the following error messages:
80|
81|```{testsetup} class
82|@define
83|class Class:
84|    a_list: list[int]
85|    a_dict: dict[str, int]
86|```
87|
88|```{doctest} class
89|
90|>>> from cattrs import structure, transform_error
91|
92|>>> try:
93|...     structure({"a_list": ["a"], "a_dict": {"str": "a"}}, Class)
94|... except Exception as exc:
95|...     print(transform_error(exc))
96|['invalid value for type, expected int @ $.a_list[0]', "invalid value for type, expected int @ $.a_dict['str']"]
97|```
98|
99|A small number of built-in exceptions are converted into error messages automatically.
100|This can be further customized by providing {func}`cattrs.transform_error` with a function that it can use to turn individual, non-ExceptionGroup exceptions into error messages.
101|A useful pattern is wrapping the default, {func}`cattrs.v.format_exception` function.
102|
103|```
104|>>> from cattrs.v import format_exception
105|
106|>>> def my_exception_formatter(exc: BaseException, type) -> str:
107|...     if isinstance(exc, MyInterestingException):
108|...         return "My error message"
109|...     return format_exception(exc, type)
110|
111|>>> try:
112|...     structure(..., Class)
113|... except Exception as exc:
114|...     print(transform_error(exc, format_exception=my_exception_formatter))
115|```
116|
117|If even more customization is required, {func}`cattrs.transform_error` can be copied over into your codebase and adjusted as needed.
118|
119|## Non-detailed Validation
120|
121|Non-detailed validation can be enabled by initializing any of the converters with `detailed_validation=False`.
122|In this mode, any errors during un/structuring will bubble up directly as soon as they happen.

1|# Why *cattrs*?
2|
3|Python has a rich set of powerful, easy to use, built-in **unstructured** data types like dictionaries, lists and tuples.
4|These data types effortlessly convert into common serialization formats like JSON, MessagePack, CBOR, YAML or TOML.
5|
6|But the data that is used by your **business logic** should be **structured** into well-defined classes, since not all combinations of field names or values are valid inputs to your programs.
7|The more trust you can have into the structure of your data, the simpler your code can be, and the fewer edge cases you have to worry about.
8|
9|When you're handed unstructured data (by your network, file system, database, ...), _cattrs_ helps to convert this data into trustworthy structured data.
10|When you have to convert your structured data into data types that other libraries can handle, _cattrs_ turns your classes and enumerations into dictionaries, integers and strings.
11|
12|_attrs_ (and to a certain degree dataclasses) are excellent libraries for declaratively describing the structure of your data, but they're purposefully not serialization libraries.
13|*cattrs* is there for you the moment your `attrs.asdict(your_instance)` and `YourClass(**data)` start failing you because you need more control over the conversion process.
14|
15|
16|## Examples
17|
18|```{include} ../README.md
19|:start-after: "begin-example -->"
20|:end-before: "<!-- end-example"
21|```
22|
23|:::{important}
24|Note how the structuring and unstructuring details do **not** pollute your class, meaning: your data model.
25|Any needs to configure the conversion are done within *cattrs* itself, not within your data model.
26|
27|There are popular validation libraries for Python that couple your data model with its validation and serialization rules based on, for example, web APIs.
28|We think that's the wrong approach.
29|Validation and serializations are concerns of the edges of your program – not the core.
30|They should neither apply design pressure on your business code, nor affect the performance of your code through unnecessary validation.
31|In bigger real-world code bases it's also common for data coming from multiple sources that need different validation and serialization rules.
32|
33|🎶 You gotta keep 'em separated. 🎶
34|:::
35|
36|
37|*cattrs* also works with the usual Python collection types like dictionaries, lists, or tuples when you want to **normalize** unstructured data data into a certain (still unstructured) shape.
38|For example, to convert a list of a float, an int and a string into a tuple of ints:
39|
40|```python
41|>>> import cattrs
42|
43|>>> cattrs.structure([1.0, 2, "3"], tuple[int, int, int])
44|(1, 2, 3)
45|
46|```
47|
48|Finally, here's a much more complex example, involving _attrs_ classes where _cattrs_ interprets the type annotations to structure and unstructure the data correctly, including Enums and nested data structures:
49|
50|```python
51|>>> from enum import unique, Enum
52|>>> from typing import Sequence
53|>>> from cattrs import structure, unstructure
54|>>> from attrs import define, field
55|
56|>>> @unique
57|... class CatBreed(Enum):
58|...     SIAMESE = "siamese"
59|...     MAINE_COON = "maine_coon"
60|...     SACRED_BIRMAN = "birman"
61|
62|>>> @define
63|... class Cat:
64|...     breed: CatBreed
65|...     names: Sequence[str]
66|
67|>>> @define
68|... class DogMicrochip:
69|...     chip_id = field()  # Type annotations are optional, but recommended
70|...     time_chipped: float = field()
71|
72|>>> @define
73|... class Dog:
74|...     cuteness: int
75|...     chip: DogMicrochip | None = None
76|
77|>>> p = unstructure([Dog(cuteness=1, chip=DogMicrochip(chip_id=1, time_chipped=10.0)),
78|...                  Cat(breed=CatBreed.MAINE_COON, names=('Fluffly', 'Fluffer'))])
79|
80|>>> p
81|[{'cuteness': 1, 'chip': {'chip_id': 1, 'time_chipped': 10.0}}, {'breed': 'maine_coon', 'names': ['Fluffly', 'Fluffer']}]
82|>>> structure(p, list[Dog | Cat])
83|[Dog(cuteness=1, chip=DogMicrochip(chip_id=1, time_chipped=10.0)), Cat(breed=<CatBreed.MAINE_COON: 'maine_coon'>, names=['Fluffly', 'Fluffer'])]
84|
85|```
86|
87|:::{tip}
88|Consider unstructured data a low-level representation that needs to be converted to structured data to be handled, and use `structure()`.
89|When you're done, `unstructure()` the data to its unstructured form and pass it along to another library or module.
90|:::
91|

94|:start-after: "begin-why -->"
95|:end-before: "<!-- end-why"
96|```

1|"""Strategy for using class-specific (un)structuring methods."""
2|
3|from inspect import signature
4|from typing import Any, Callable, Optional, TypeVar
5|
6|from .. import BaseConverter
7|
8|T = TypeVar("T")
9|
10|
11|def use_class_methods(
12|    converter: BaseConverter,
13|    structure_method_name: Optional[str] = None,
14|    unstructure_method_name: Optional[str] = None,
15|) -> None:
16|    """
17|    Configure the converter such that dedicated methods are used for (un)structuring
18|    the instance of a class if such methods are available. The default (un)structuring
19|    will be applied if such an (un)structuring methods cannot be found.
20|
21|    :param converter: The `Converter` on which this strategy is applied. You can use
22|        :class:`cattrs.BaseConverter` or any other derived class.
23|    :param structure_method_name: Optional string with the name of the class method
24|        which should be used for structuring. If not provided, no class method will be
25|        used for structuring.
26|    :param unstructure_method_name: Optional string with the name of the class method
27|        which should be used for unstructuring. If not provided, no class method will
28|        be used for unstructuring.
29|
30|    If you want to (un)structured nested objects, just append a converter parameter
31|    to your (un)structuring methods and you will receive the converter there.
32|
33|    .. versionadded:: 23.2.0
34|    """
35|
36|    if structure_method_name:
37|
38|        def make_class_method_structure(cl: type[T]) -> Callable[[Any, type[T]], T]:
39|            fn = getattr(cl, structure_method_name)
40|            n_parameters = len(signature(fn).parameters)
41|            if n_parameters == 1:
42|                return lambda v, _: fn(v)
43|            if n_parameters == 2:
44|                return lambda v, _: fn(v, converter)
45|            raise TypeError("Provide a class method with one or two arguments.")
46|
47|        converter.register_structure_hook_factory(
48|            lambda t: hasattr(t, structure_method_name), make_class_method_structure
49|        )
50|
51|    if unstructure_method_name:
52|
53|        def make_class_method_unstructure(cl: type[T]) -> Callable[[T], T]:
54|            fn = getattr(cl, unstructure_method_name)
55|            n_parameters = len(signature(fn).parameters)
56|            if n_parameters == 1:
57|                return fn
58|            if n_parameters == 2:
59|                return lambda self_: fn(self_, converter)
60|            raise TypeError("Provide a method with no or one argument.")
61|
62|        converter.register_unstructure_hook_factory(
63|            lambda t: hasattr(t, unstructure_method_name), make_class_method_unstructure
64|        )

--- FILE: docs/recipes.md ---
1|# Recipes
2|
3|This page contains a collection of recipes for custom un-/structuring mechanisms.
4|
5|
6|## Switching Initializers
7|
8|When structuring _attrs_ classes, _cattrs_ uses the classes' ``__init__`` method to instantiate objects by default.
9|In certain situations, you might want to deviate from this behavior and use alternative initializers instead.
10|
11|For example, consider the following `Point` class describing points in 2D space, which offers two `classmethod`s for alternative creation:
12|
13|```{doctest} point_group
14|>>> import math
15|>>> from attrs import define
16|
17|>>> @define
18|... class Point:
19|...     """A point in 2D space."""
20|...     x: float
21|...     y: float
22|...
23|...     @classmethod
24|...     def from_tuple(cls, coordinates: tuple[float, float]) -> "Point":
25|...         """Create a point from a tuple of Cartesian coordinates."""
26|...         return Point(*coordinates)
27|...
28|...     @classmethod
29|...     def from_polar(cls, radius: float, angle: float) -> "Point":
30|...         """Create a point from its polar coordinates."""
31|...         return Point(radius * math.cos(angle), radius * math.sin(angle))
32|```
33|
34|
35|### Selecting an Alternative Initializer
36|
37|A simple way to _statically_ set one of the `classmethod`s as initializer is to register a structuring hook that holds a reference to the respective callable:
38|
39|```{doctest} point_group
40|>>> from inspect import signature
41|>>> from typing import Callable, TypedDict
42|
43|>>> from cattrs import Converter
44|>>> from cattrs.dispatch import StructureHook
45|
46|>>> def signature_to_typed_dict(fn: Callable) -> type[TypedDict]:
47|...     """Create a TypedDict reflecting a callable's signature."""
48|...     params = {p: t.annotation for p, t in signature(fn).parameters.items()}
49|...     return TypedDict(f"{fn.__name__}_args", params)
50|...
51|
52|>>> def make_initializer_from(fn: Callable, conv: Converter) -> StructureHook:
53|...     """Return a structuring hook from a given callable."""
54|...     td = signature_to_typed_dict(fn)
55|...     td_hook = conv.get_structure_hook(td)
56|...     return lambda v, _: fn(**td_hook(v, td))
57|```
58|
59|Now, you can easily structure `Point`s from the specified alternative representation:
60|
61|```{doctest} point_group
62|>>> c = Converter()
63|>>> c.register_structure_hook(Point, make_initializer_from(Point.from_polar, c))
64|
65|>>> p0 = Point(1.0, 0.0)
66|>>> p1 = c.structure({"radius": 1.0, "angle": 0.0}, Point)
67|>>> assert p0 == p1
68|```
69|
70|
71|### Dynamically Switching Between Initializers
72|
73|In some cases, even more flexibility is required and the selection of the initializer must happen at runtime, requiring a dynamic approach.
74|A typical scenario would be when object structuring happens behind an API and you want to let the user specify which representation of the object they wish to provide in their serialization string.
75|
76|In such situations, the following hook factory can help you achieve your goal:
77|
78|```{doctest} point_group
79|>>> from inspect import signature
80|>>> from typing import Callable, TypedDict
81|
82|>>> from cattrs import Converter
83|>>> from cattrs.dispatch import StructureHook
84|
85|>>> def signature_to_typed_dict(fn: Callable) -> type[TypedDict]:
86|...     """Create a TypedDict reflecting a callable's signature."""
87|...     params = {p: t.annotation for p, t in signature(fn).parameters.items()}
88|...     return TypedDict(f"{fn.__name__}_args", params)
89|
90|>>> T = TypeVar("T")
91|>>> def make_initializer_selection_hook(
92|...     initializer_key: str,
93|...     converter: Converter,
94|... ) -> StructureHook:
95|...     """Return a structuring hook that dynamically switches between initializers."""
96|...
97|...     def select_initializer_hook(specs: dict, cls: type[T]) -> T:
98|...         """Deserialization with dynamic initializer selection."""
99|...
100|...         # If no initializer keyword is specified, use regular __init__
101|...         if initializer_key not in specs:
102|...             return converter.structure_attrs_fromdict(specs, cls)
103|...
104|...         # Otherwise, call the specified initializer with deserialized arguments
105|...         specs = specs.copy()
106|...         initializer_name = specs.pop(initializer_key)
107|...         initializer = getattr(cls, initializer_name)
108|...         td = signature_to_typed_dict(initializer)
109|...         td_hook = converter.get_structure_hook(td)
110|...         return initializer(**td_hook(specs, td))
111|...
112|...     return select_initializer_hook
113|```
114|
115|Specifying the key that determines the initializer to be used now lets you dynamically select the `classmethod` as part of the object specification itself:
116|
117|```{doctest} point_group
118|>>> c = Converter()
119|>>> c.register_structure_hook(Point, make_initializer_selection_hook("initializer", c))
120|
121|>>> p0 = Point(1.0, 0.0)
122|>>> p1 = c.structure({"initializer": "from_polar", "radius": 1.0, "angle": 0.0}, Point)
123|>>> p2 = c.structure({"initializer": "from_tuple", "coordinates": (1.0, 0.0)}, Point)
124|>>> assert p0 == p1 == p2
125|```

6|
7|from cbor2 import dumps, loads

9|

13|from ..strategies import configure_union_passthrough
14|from . import (
15|    is_primitive_enum,
16|    literals_with_enums_unstructure_factory,
17|    unstructure_datetime_as_timestamp,
18|    wrap,
19|)
20|
21|T = TypeVar("T")
22|
23|
24|class Cbor2Converter(Converter):
25|    def dumps(self, obj: Any, unstructure_as: Any = None, **kwargs: Any) -> bytes:
26|        return dumps(self.unstructure(obj, unstructure_as=unstructure_as), **kwargs)
27|
28|    def loads(self, data: bytes, cl: TypeForm[T], **kwargs: Any) -> T:
29|        """Deserialize and structure the provided data as ``cl``.
30|
31|        .. versionchanged:: NEXT
32|            The target type is now annotated with ``TypeForm`` to support
33|            stronger typing.
34|        """
35|        return self.structure(loads(data, **kwargs), cl)
36|
37|
38|def configure_converter(converter: BaseConverter):
39|    """
40|    Configure the converter for use with the cbor2 library.
41|
42|    * datetimes are serialized as timestamp floats
43|    * sets are serialized as lists
44|    * string and int enums are passed through when unstructuring
45|    """
46|    converter.register_unstructure_hook(datetime, unstructure_datetime_as_timestamp)
47|    converter.register_structure_hook(
48|        datetime, lambda v, _: datetime.fromtimestamp(v, timezone.utc)
49|    )
50|    converter.register_unstructure_hook(date, lambda v: v.isoformat())
51|    converter.register_structure_hook(date, lambda v, _: date.fromisoformat(v))
52|    converter.register_unstructure_hook_factory(is_primitive_enum, lambda t: identity)
53|    converter.register_unstructure_hook_factory(
54|        is_literal_containing_enums, literals_with_enums_unstructure_factory
55|    )
56|    configure_union_passthrough(Union[str, bool, int, float, None, bytes], converter)
57|
58|
59|@wrap(Cbor2Converter)
60|def make_converter(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Cbor2Converter:
61|    kwargs["unstruct_collection_overrides"] = {
62|        Set: list,
63|        **kwargs.get("unstruct_collection_overrides", {}),
64|    }
65|    res = Cbor2Converter(*args, **kwargs)

1|# Handling Unions
2|
3|_cattrs_ is able to handle simple unions of _attrs_ classes and dataclasses [automatically](#default-union-strategy).
4|More complex cases require converter customization (since there are many ways of handling unions).
5|
6|_cattrs_ also comes with a number of optional strategies to help handle unions:
7|
8|- [tagged unions strategy](strategies.md#tagged-unions-strategy) mentioned below
9|- [union passthrough strategy](strategies.md#union-passthrough), which is preapplied to all the [preconfigured](preconf.md) converters
10|
11|## Default Union Strategy
12|
13|For convenience, _cattrs_ includes a default union structuring strategy which is a little more opinionated.
14|
15|Given a union of several _attrs_ classes and/or dataclasses, the default union strategy will attempt to handle it in several ways.
16|
17|First, it will look for `Literal` fields.
18|If _all members_ of the union contain a literal field, _cattrs_ will generate a disambiguation function based on the field.
19|
20|```python
21|from typing import Literal
22|
23|@define
24|class ClassA:
25|    field_one: Literal["one"]
26|
27|@define
28|class ClassB:
29|    field_one: Literal["two"] = "two"
30|```
31|
32|In this case, a payload containing `{"field_one": "one"}` will produce an instance of `ClassA`.
33|
34|````{note}
35|The following snippet can be used to disable the use of literal fields, restoring legacy behavior.
36|
37|```python
38|from functools import partial
39|from cattrs.disambiguators import is_supported_union
40|
41|converter.register_structure_hook_factory(
42|    is_supported_union,
43|    partial(converter._gen_attrs_union_structure, use_literals=False),
44|)
45|```
46|
47|````
48|
49|If there are no appropriate fields, the strategy will examine the classes for **unique required fields**.
50|
51|So, given a union of `ClassA` and `ClassB`:
52|
53|```python
54|@define
55|class ClassA:
56|    field_one: str
57|    field_with_default: str = "a default"
58|
59|@define
60|class ClassB:
61|    field_two: str
62|```
63|
64|the strategy will determine that if a payload contains the key `field_one` it should be handled as `ClassA`, and if it contains the key `field_two` it should be handled as `ClassB`.
65|The field `field_with_default` will not be considered since it has a default value, so it gets treated as optional.
66|
67|```{versionchanged} 23.2.0
68|Literals can now be potentially used to disambiguate.
69|```
70|
71|```{versionchanged} 24.1.0
72|Dataclasses are now supported in addition to _attrs_ classes.
73|```
74|
75|## Unstructuring Unions with Extra Metadata
76|
77|```{note}
78|_cattrs_ comes with the [tagged unions strategy](strategies.md#tagged-unions-strategy) for handling this exact use-case since version 23.1.
79|The example below has been left here for educational purposes, but you should prefer the strategy.
80|```
81|
82|Let's assume a simple scenario of two classes, `ClassA` and `ClassB`, both
83|of which have no distinct fields and so cannot be used automatically with
84|_cattrs_.
85|
86|```python
87|@define
88|class ClassA:
89|    a_string: str
90|
91|@define
92|class ClassB:
93|    a_string: str
94|```
95|
96|A naive approach to unstructuring either of these would yield identical
97|dictionaries, and not enough information to restructure the classes.
98|
99|```python
100|>>> converter.unstructure(ClassA("test"))
101|{'a_string': 'test'}  # Is this ClassA or ClassB? Who knows!
102|```
103|
104|What we can do is ensure some extra information is present in the
105|unstructured data, and then use that information to help structure later.
106|
107|First, we register an unstructure hook for the `Union[ClassA, ClassB]` type.
108|
109|```python
110|>>> converter.register_unstructure_hook(
111|...     Union[ClassA, ClassB],
112|...     lambda o: {"_type": type(o).__name__,  **converter.unstructure(o)}
113|... )
114|>>> converter.unstructure(ClassA("test"), unstructure_as=Union[ClassA, ClassB])
115|{'_type': 'ClassA', 'a_string': 'test'}
116|```
117|
118|Note that when unstructuring, we had to provide the `unstructure_as` parameter
119|or _cattrs_ would have just applied the usual unstructuring rules to `ClassA`,
120|instead of our special union hook.
121|
122|Now that the unstructured data contains some information, we can create a
123|structuring hook to put it to use:
124|
125|```python
126|>>> converter.register_structure_hook(
127|...     Union[ClassA, ClassB],
128|...     lambda o, _: converter.structure(o, ClassA if o["_type"] == "ClassA" else ClassB)
129|... )
130|>>> converter.structure({"_type": "ClassA", "a_string": "test"}, Union[ClassA, ClassB])
131|ClassA(a_string='test')
132|```

--- FILE: docs/basics.md ---
1|# The Basics
2|```{currentmodule} cattrs
3|```
4|
5|All _cattrs_ functionality is exposed through a {class}`cattrs.Converter` object.
6|A global converter is provided for convenience as {data}`cattrs.global_converter`
7|but more complex customizations should be performed on private instances, any number of which can be made.
8|
9|
10|## Converters and Hooks
11|
12|The core functionality of a converter is structuring and unstructuring data by composing [provided](defaulthooks.md) and [custom handling functions](customizing.md), called _hooks_.
13|
14|To create a private converter, instantiate a {class}`cattrs.Converter`. Converters are relatively cheap; users are encouraged to have as many as they need.
15|
16|The two main methods, {meth}`structure <cattrs.BaseConverter.structure>` and {meth}`unstructure <cattrs.BaseConverter.unstructure>`, are used to convert between _structured_ and _unstructured_ data.
17|
18|```{doctest} basics
19|>>> from cattrs import structure, unstructure
20|>>> from attrs import define
21|
22|>>> @define
23|... class Model:
24|...    a: int
25|
26|>>> unstructure(Model(1))
27|{'a': 1}
28|>>> structure({"a": 1}, Model)
29|Model(a=1)
30|```
31|
32|_cattrs_ comes with a rich library of un/structuring hooks by default but it excels at composing custom hooks with built-in ones.
33|
34|The simplest approach to customization is writing a new hook from scratch.
35|For example, we can write our own hook for the `int` class and register it to a converter.
36|
37|```{doctest} basics
38|>>> from cattrs import Converter
39|
40|>>> converter = Converter()
41|
42|>>> @converter.register_structure_hook
43|... def int_hook(value, type) -> int:
44|...     if not isinstance(value, int):
45|...         raise ValueError('not an int!')
46|...     return value
47|```
48|
49|Now, any other hook converting an `int` will use it.
50|
51|Another approach to customization is wrapping (composing) an existing hook with your own function.
52|A base hook can be obtained from a converter and then be subjected to the very rich machinery of function composition that Python offers.
53|
54|
55|```{doctest} basics
56|>>> base_hook = converter.get_structure_hook(Model)
57|
58|>>> @converter.register_structure_hook
59|... def my_model_hook(value, type) -> Model:
60|...     # Apply any preprocessing to the value.
61|...     result = base_hook(value, type)
62|...     # Apply any postprocessing to the model.
63|...     return result
64|```
65|
66|(`cattrs.structure({}, Model)` is equivalent to `cattrs.get_structure_hook(Model)({}, Model)`.)
67|
68|Now if we use this hook to structure a `Model`, through ✨the magic of function composition✨ that hook will use our old `int_hook`.
69|
70|```python
71|>>> converter.structure({"a": "1"}, Model)
72|  + Exception Group Traceback (most recent call last):
73|    |   File "...", line 22, in <module>
74|    |     base_hook({"a": "1"}, Model)
75|    |   File "<cattrs generated structure __main__.Model>", line 9, in structure_Model
76|    | cattrs.errors.ClassValidationError: While structuring Model (1 sub-exception)
77|    +-+---------------- 1 ----------------
78|      | Traceback (most recent call last):
79|      |   File "<cattrs generated structure __main__.Model>", line 5, in structure_Model
80|      |   File "...", line 15, in my_int_hook
81|      |     raise ValueError("not an int!")
82|      | ValueError: not an int!
83|      | Structuring class Model @ attribute a
84|      +------------------------------------
85|```
86|
87|To continue reading about customizing _cattrs_, see [](customizing.md).
88|More advanced structuring customizations are commonly called [](strategies.md).
89|
90|## Global Converter
91|
92|Global _cattrs_ functions, such as {meth}`cattrs.structure`, use a single {data}`global converter <cattrs.global_converter>`.
93|Changes done to this global converter, such as registering new structure and unstructure hooks, affect all code using the global functions.
94|
95|The following functions implicitly use this global converter:
96|
97|- {meth}`cattrs.structure`
98|- {meth}`cattrs.unstructure`
99|- {meth}`cattrs.get_structure_hook`
100|- {meth}`cattrs.get_unstructure_hook`
101|- {meth}`cattrs.structure_attrs_fromtuple`
102|- {meth}`cattrs.structure_attrs_fromdict`
103|
104|Changes made to the global converter will affect the behavior of these functions.
105|
106|Larger applications are strongly encouraged to create and customize different, private instances of {class}`cattrs.Converter`.

--- FILE: CONTRIBUTING.md ---
1|# Contributing
2|
3|Contributions are welcome, and they are greatly appreciated!
4|Every little bit helps, and credit will always be given.
5|
6|> [!IMPORTANT]
7|> If you use LLM / "AI" tools for your contributions, please read and follow our [_Generative AI / LLM Policy_][llm].
8|
9|You can contribute in many ways:
10|
11|## Types of Contributions
12|
13|### Report Bugs
14|
15|Report bugs at [https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs/issues](https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs/issues).
16|
17|If you are reporting a bug, please include:
18|
19|- Your operating system name and version.
20|- Any details about your local setup that might be helpful in troubleshooting.
21|- Detailed steps to reproduce the bug.
22|
23|### Fix Bugs
24|
25|Look through the GitHub issues for bugs. Anything tagged with "bug"
26|and "help wanted" is open to whoever wants to implement it.
27|
28|### Implement Features
29|
30|Look through the GitHub issues for features.
31|Anything tagged with "enhancement" and "help wanted" is open to whoever wants to implement it.
32|
33|### Write Documentation
34|
35|_cattrs_ could always use more documentation, whether as part of the
36|official cattrs docs, in docstrings, or even on the web in blog posts,
37|articles, and such.
38|
39|### Submit Feedback
40|
41|The best way to send feedback is to file an issue at [https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs/issues](https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs/issues).
42|
43|If you are proposing a feature:
44|
45|- Explain in detail how it would work.
46|- Keep the scope as narrow as possible, to make it easier to implement.
47|- Remember that this is a volunteer-driven project, and that contributions
48|  are welcome :)
49|
50|## Get Started!
51|
52|Ready to contribute? Here's how to set up _cattrs_ for local development.
53|
54|1. Fork the `cattrs` repo on GitHub.
55|2. Clone your fork locally::
56|
57|```shell
58|$ git clone git@github.com:your_name_here/cattrs.git
59|```
60|
61|3. Install your local copy into a virtualenv. Assuming you have [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) installed, this is how you set up your fork for local development::
62|
63|```shell
64|$ cd cattrs/
65|$ uv sync --all-groups --all-extras
66|```
67|
68|4. Create a branch for local development::
69|
70|```shell
71|$ git switch -c name-of-your-bugfix-or-feature
72|```
73|
74|Now you can make your changes locally.
75|
76|5. When you're done making changes, check that your changes pass lints and the tests, including testing other Python versions::
77|
78|```shell
79|$ just lint
80|$ just test
81|$ just --set python python3.10 test  # Test on other versions
82|```
83|
84|6. Write any necessary documentation, including updating the changelog (HISTORY.md). The docs can be built like so:
85|
86|```shell
87|$ just docs
88|$ just htmllive  # Build the docs, serve then and autoreload on changes
89|```
90|
91|7. Commit your changes and push your branch to GitHub::
92|
93|```shell
94|$ git add .
95|$ git commit -m "Your detailed description of your changes."
96|$ git push origin name-of-your-bugfix-or-feature
97|```
98|
99|8. Submit a pull request through the GitHub website.
100|
101|## Pull Request Guidelines
102|
103|Before you submit a pull request, check that it meets these guidelines:
104|
105|1. **Only contribute code that you fully understand.**
106|   See also our [AI policy][llm].
107|2. The pull request should include tests.
108|3. If the pull request adds functionality, the docs should be updated. Put
109|   your new functionality into a function with a docstring, and add the
110|   feature to the list in README.rst.
111|4. The pull request should work for all supported Python versions. Check
112|   [https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs/actions](https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs/actions)
113|   and make sure that the tests pass for all supported Python versions.
114|5. Don't forget to add a line to HISTORY.md.
115|
116|## Tips
117|
118|To run a subset of tests:
119|
120|```shell
121|$ just test tests/test_unstructure.py
122|```
123|
124|Static typing tests live in `tests/test_typing_structure.md` and run through `pytest-typing` with Mypy and Pyrefly on CPython 3.14.
125|To run them on their own:
126|
127|```shell
128|$ just --set python python3.14 test tests/test_typing_structure.md
129|```
130|
131|The test dependencies pin both checkers in `uv.lock`, including a Mypy version with `TypeForm` support enabled by default.
132|`pytest-typing` is configured to use Pyrefly's `strict` preset for the temporary test snippets.
133|
134|[llm]: https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs/blob/main/.github/AI_POLICY.md

1|# Migrations
2|
3|```{currentmodule} cattrs
4|```
5|
6|_cattrs_ sometimes changes in backwards-incompatible ways.
7|This page contains guidance for changes and workarounds for restoring legacy behavior.
8|
9|## 26.2.0
10|
11|### Naive datetimes unstructuring as UTC in the _msgpack_ and _cbor2_ converters
12|
13|The _msgpack_ and _cbor2_ converters unstructure `datetime` s into UNIX timestamps using `datetime.timestamp`, which reads a naive `datetime` as local time.
14|The serialized value therefore depended on the timezone of the machine doing the unstructuring, while the structure hooks read timestamps back as UTC.
15|From this version on, naive `datetime` s are assumed to be UTC when unstructuring, so both ends of the round-trip agree and the payload no longer depends on the host.
16|
17|Aware `datetime` s are unaffected.
18|
19|The old behavior can be restored by registering `datetime.timestamp` directly on a converter.
20|
21|```python
22|>>> from datetime import datetime
23|
24|>>> converter.register_unstructure_hook(datetime, datetime.timestamp)
25|```
26|
27|## 25.3.0
28|
29|### Abstract sets structuring into frozensets
30|
31|From this version on, abstract sets (`collection.abc.Set`) structure into frozensets.
32|
33|The old behavior can be restored by registering the {meth}`BaseConverter._structure_set <cattrs.BaseConverter._structure_set>` method using the {meth}`is_abstract_set <cattrs.cols.is_abstract_set>` predicate on a converter.
34|
35|```python
36|>>> from cattrs.cols import is_abstract_set
37|
38|>>> converter.register_structure_hook_func(is_abstract_set, converter._structure_set)
39|```
40|
41|## 25.2.0
42|
43|### Sequences structuring into tuples
44|
45|Sequences were changed to structure into tuples instead of lists.
46|
47|The old behavior can be restored by registering the `list_structure_factory` using the `is_sequence` predicate on a converter.
48|
49|```python
50|>>> from cattrs.cols import is_sequence, list_structure_factory
51|
52|>>> converter.register_structure_hook_factory(is_sequence, list_structure_factory)
53|```
54|
55|## 25.1.0
56|
57|### The default structure hook fallback factory
58|
59|The default structure hook fallback factory was changed to more eagerly raise errors for missing hooks.
60|
61|The old behavior can be restored by explicitly passing in the old hook fallback factory when instantiating the converter.
62|
63|
64|```python
65|>>> from cattrs.fns import raise_error
66|
67|>>> c = Converter(structure_fallback_factory=lambda _: raise_error)
68|# Or
69|>>> c = BaseConverter(structure_fallback_factory=lambda _: raise_error)
70|```
71|
72|### `cattrs.gen.MappingStructureFn` and `cattrs.gen.DictStructureFn` removal
73|
74|The internal `cattrs.gen.MappingStructureFn` and `cattrs.gen.DictStructureFn` types were replaced by a more general type, `cattrs.SimpleStructureHook[In, T]`.
75|If you were using `MappingStructureFn`, use `SimpleStructureHook[Mapping[Any, Any], T]` instead.
76|If you were using `DictStructureFn`, use `SimpleStructureHook[Mapping[str, Any], T]` instead.
--- END FILE: docs/migrations.md ---

1|# Benchmarking
2|
3|cattrs includes a benchmarking suite to help detect performance regressions and
4|guide performance optimizations.
5|
6|The suite is based on pytest and pytest-benchmark. Benchmarks are similar to
7|tests, with the exception of being stored in the `bench/` directory and being
8|used to verify performance instead of correctness.
9|
10|## A Sample Workflow
11|
12|First, ensure the system you're benchmarking on is as stable as possible. For
13|example, the pyperf library has a `system tune` command that can tweak
14|CPU frequency governors. You also might want to quit as many applications as
15|possible and run the benchmark suite on isolated CPU cores (`taskset` can be
16|used for this purpose on Linux).
17|
18|Then, generate a baseline using `make bench`. This will run the benchmark suite
19|and save it into a file.
20|
21|Following that, implement the changes you have in mind. Run the test suite to
22|ensure correctness. Then, compare the performance of the new code to the saved
23|baseline using `make bench-cmp`. If the code is still correct but faster,
24|congratulations!
--- END FILE: docs/benchmarking.md ---

153|def gen_attr_names() -> Iterable[str]:
154|    """
155|    Generate names for attributes, 'a'...'z', then 'aa'...'zz'.
156|    ~702 different attribute names should be enough in practice.
157|    Some short strings (such as 'as') are keywords, so we skip them.
158|
159|    Every second attribute name is private (starts with an underscore).
160|    """
161|    lc = string.ascii_lowercase
162|    has_underscore = False
163|    for c in lc:
164|        yield c if not has_underscore else "_" + c
165|        has_underscore = not has_underscore
166|    for outer in lc:
167|        for inner in lc:
168|            res = outer + inner
169|            if keyword.iskeyword(res):
170|                continue
171|            yield outer + inner

174|def _create_hyp_class(
175|    attrs_and_strategy: list[tuple[_CountingAttr, st.SearchStrategy[PosArgs]]],
176|    frozen=None,
177|) -> SearchStrategy[AttrsAndArgs]:
178|    """
179|    A helper function for Hypothesis to generate attrs classes.
180|
181|    The result is a tuple: an attrs class, a tuple of values to
182|    instantiate it, and a kwargs dict for kw-only attributes.

185|    def key(t):
186|        return (t[0].default is not NOTHING, t[0].kw_only or False)

188|    attrs_and_strat = sorted(attrs_and_strategy, key=key)
189|    attrs = [a[0] for a in attrs_and_strat]
190|    for i, a in enumerate(attrs):

195|        if attr_and_strat[0].kw_only:

198|            kwargs[attr_name] = attr_and_strat[1]

200|        st.builds(
201|            lambda f: make_class(
202|                "HypClass", dict(zip(gen_attr_names(), attrs)), frozen=f
203|            ),
204|            st.booleans() if frozen is None else st.just(frozen),
205|        ),
206|        st.tuples(*vals),
207|        st.fixed_dictionaries(kwargs),

307|    a strategy for building classes that have as an attribute:
308|        * just the simpler class
309|        * a list of simpler classes

314|    # class strategy>).

196|def _create_hyp_class(

199|) -> SearchStrategy[tuple[type, PosArgs, KwArgs]]:
200|    """
201|    A helper function for Hypothesis to generate attrs classes.
202|
203|    The result is a tuple: an attrs class, tuple of values to
204|    instantiate it, and a kwargs dict for kw_only args.
205|    """
206|
207|    def key(t):
208|        return (t[0]._default is not NOTHING, t[0].kw_only)
209|
210|    attrs_and_strat = sorted(attrs_and_strategy, key=key)
211|    attrs = [a[0] for a in attrs_and_strat]
212|    for i, a in enumerate(attrs):
213|        a.counter = i
214|    vals = tuple((a[1]) for a in attrs_and_strat if not a[0].kw_only)
215|    note(f"Class fields: {attrs}")
216|    attrs_dict = {}
217|
218|    names = gen_attr_names()
219|    kwarg_strats = {}
220|
221|    for ix, (attribute, strat) in enumerate(attrs_and_strat):
222|        name = next(names)

224|        if ix % 2 == 1:
225|            # Every third attribute gets an alias, the next attribute name.

240|        tuples(*vals),
